newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rate hike odds lengthen after April PPI drops.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rate hike odds lengthen after April PPI drops.

text.p: The Federal Reserve on Wednesday got yet another reason to leave interest rates steady next week: non-existent wholesale inflation pressures for as far as the eye can see.
The Labor Department reported that the April Producer Price index (PPI) fell an unexpected 0.6 percent in April, while the PPI ex-food and energy dipped 0.1 percent.
Not since August 1993 had the PPI fallen so much in a month. The drop led analysts to say that the odds of another Fed interest-rate hike next week have substantially declined.
The Fed "is going to have to do a little more explaining if they do move (rates higher)," said Louis Crandall, chief economist at R.H. Wrightson & Associates.
Indeed, virtually every category in the PPI was down in April, led by a 2.6 percent fall in energy prices.
"It's a fantastic report," said Fred Levin, chief economist at Eastbridge Capital Markets. "There is no inflation (now) and no pipeline inflation pressures."
Analysts pointed to declines in both crude and intermediate goods prices as reasons to have no fears about wholesale inflation surfacing anytime soon.
Overall crude prices fell 0.9 percent, with the crude "core" down 2.3 percent. Intermediate prices fell 0.3 percent in April, with its core rate unchanged.
April's data follows a 6.9 percent fall in overall crude prices and a 0.6 percent rise in "core" crude prices in March, and a 0.6 fall in overall intermediate prices and flat "core" rate in March.
At the finished goods level, the PPI was down 0.1 percent in March, but the "core" rate was up 0.4 percent.
The March core figure, though, was viewed as skewed by an unusual increase in aircraft prices.
But analysts noted that the extremely favorable total April PPI would be unlikely to continue, since energy prices are expected to stabilize.
Crandall noted that the big drop in energy prices was a "payback" for the increases seen in the winter.

Still, core PPI was up a scant 0.2 percent for the first four months of the year, analysts said. And, they said, core PPI was up just 0.6 percent over April 1996, with the total PPI up 0.8 percent from a year ago.
"Everyone is waiting for the trend in PPI to change but it's not happening," Crandall said.
The tame inflation data bouyed bond prices. The 30-year bond jumped nearly 3/4-point, sending its yield down to 6.87 percent.
Gains, though, were capped since the market believes that the Fed is looking less at inflation data and more at demand.
